title: He didn’t negotiate with demons.
paragraphs:
He didn’t negotiate with demons.
He exposed them.
And what happened next will disturb you—if you really see it.

A man lived where no one else would dare to stay.
Among tombs. Among bones. Among silence and screams.
He wasn’t just broken.
He was occupied.

Chains couldn’t hold him.
People couldn’t help him.
Society had already labeled him: too far gone.
But then…
Jesus stepped onto the shore.
Before anyone could explain the situation—before the disciples could even ask questions—the demons inside the man recognized Him.

Not as teacher.
Not as prophet.
But as Lord.
They begged.
Let that sink in.

Everything that once dominated this man…
Everything that made him cut himself, isolate himself, destroy himself…
…was now begging.

Because when Jesus shows up, darkness doesn’t negotiate.
It surrenders.
And then comes the moment that confuses many.

The demons ask to enter a herd of pigs.
Jesus allows it.
And instantly—violently—the pigs rush down the slope and drown in the sea.
Why would Jesus permit that?
Here’s the truth most people miss:
Evil always drives toward destruction.
Always.

The pigs didn’t become evil.
They revealed evil.

Because Satan doesn’t come to manage your life—he comes to ruin it.
Not slowly. Not safely.
Completely.

That addiction you’re hiding?
That secret habit?
That bitterness you keep feeding?
It doesn’t want to stay small.
It wants to consume you.
But here’s where grace interrupts the story.
Because the focus is not the pigs.
It’s the man.

The one everyone gave up on.
The one people feared more than they loved.
The one who probably forgot what freedom even felt like.
When the dust settled…
He was no longer screaming.

No longer naked.
No longer chained.
No longer lost.
Scripture says he was “sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind.” (Mark 5:15)
Let that hit your spirit.

Jesus didn’t just remove demons.
He restored dignity.

He didn’t just silence chaos.
He rebuilt identity.
And that’s the Gospel.

Not behavior modification.
Not image repair.
Total transformation.
But the story takes another turn—and it’s uncomfortable.

The people from the town came out.
They saw the man restored.
And instead of celebrating…
They were afraid.
Not of the demons.
Of Jesus.
Why?
Because deliverance had a cost.

The pigs were gone.
Their economy was shaken.
Their comfort disrupted.
And they made a choice many still make today:
They asked Jesus to leave.
Read that again.

They chose financial loss over spiritual freedom.
They preferred controlled darkness over disruptive light.
And we still do this.

We tolerate sin as long as it doesn’t cost us too much.
We avoid surrender because we’re afraid of what we might lose.
But listen—
Anything you lose to gain Christ is not loss. It’s rescue.

That man?
He begged to go with Jesus.
Who wouldn’t?
After being freed like that?
But Jesus said something unexpected:
“Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how He has had mercy on you.” (Mark 5:19)
In other words:

You were delivered publicly.
Now go testify boldly.
Your story is not your shame.
It’s your assignment.

Some of you are still sitting in silent tombs.
Smiling outside, screaming inside.

Bound—but functioning.
Occupied—but hiding it well.
Hear me clearly:
Jesus still steps onto shores.

He still crosses distances for one soul.
He still speaks with authority.
He still breaks chains that psychology, willpower, and time could never break.
You are not too far gone.

Not too addicted.
Not too dirty.
Not too damaged.
If a man filled with a legion of demons can sit peacefully at the feet of Jesus…
What makes you think your situation is beyond Him?
This is not just a story.
This is an invitation.

Come out of the tombs.
Step into the light.
Let Jesus confront what you’ve been entertaining.
Yes, it will cost you.
Yes, some “pigs” will have to go.
But freedom is worth more than everything you’re trying to keep.
And when He sets you free—
You won’t just be healed.
You’ll be sent.

From bondage to testimony.
From isolation to mission.
So here’s the question:
Do you want to keep what’s killing you… or surrender to the One who can restore you?
“We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.”
